finding: The fence -- which §2 calls 'the release's actual content' -- is specified over one of the two commands that write this field, and the surface it omits is the one the guard being reversed actually exercises. §2: '`tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` with the escalation hint'; §5 test 11 repeats the same single form. tp has two workflow write surfaces and §2's own precedence chain names both layers they write: `tp set --workflow <f>=<v>` writes the task override, `tp set --workflow --project <f>=<v>` writes `.tp/config.json`. Three independent facts say the omission is live rather than pedantic. (1) The guard §4 reverses uses the project form: `internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:472` is `runTP(t, dir, "set", "--workflow", "--project", "audit_converge_on=blocking")`, so the two assertions §4 says the release reverses are assertions about the surface §2 never fences -- a unit implementing §2 and §4 literally makes `--project` succeed and leaves it unfenced. (2) The shipped mechanism already contemplates both: `fenceWorkflowWrite`'s doc comment at internal/cli/unattended.go:50-55 says 'so both tp set --workflow and its --project form can call it on every field they parse', and the shipped `runner`/`notify_cmd` fence is 'at **any** layer' (REFERENCE.md's fence table). (3) The twin's own shipped spec covers both by name: spec/0.31.0.md:41 -- 'Both `tp set --workflow review_converge_on=<bad>` and `tp set --workflow --project review_converge_on=<bad>` validate the literal value they are about to persist'. So this release specifies a fence narrower than the precedent it cites, on the release whose stated purpose is that fence, and the gap is a supported route for an unattended unit to relax its own audit gate -- 'the failure the whole unattended-mode design exists to prevent', in §2's words. The same one-surface narrowness leaves the validation contract short: §2 says only 'rejected with the same hint machinery', while spec/0.31.0.md:41 splits exit 2 (a value on the command line) from exit 1 (a hand-edited stored layer a consuming command resolves), and §5 test 1 asserts only 'the same hint shape'.
suggestion: Write the fence over both forms -- '`tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` and `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` both exit 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`' -- and make test 11 assert both arms plus the exit-0 arm without the variable. Take spec/0.31.0.md:41's exit-code split for the invalid-value path as well, since 'the same hint machinery' does not say which code, and name `.tp/config.json` as a fenced layer explicitly so the implementer does not have to infer it from the field list.

finding: The marker §3 adopts for prospectivity does not discriminate: it was populated seven releases ago, so "the reset applies to rounds recorded from this release forward" is false for every audit round on disk. Measured: audit_record.go:213 stamps IDScheme: engine.IDSchemeSlug on every audit round it records, and reviewstate.go:44 dates that marker to v0.30.0+. All nine of v0.35.0's audit rounds carry "id_scheme": "slug" in spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json (lines 203, 213, 223, 233, 243, 253, 263, 273, 283), so engine.IsLegacyRound (reviewstate.go:503-505, r.IDScheme == "") returns FALSE for all nine. Under §3's rule -- "applies the reset only from the first marked round onward" -- every round of v0.29.0 onward is marked and the reset is retroactive across the whole corpus, which is exactly the outcome §3's own simulation says is unacceptable (blocking 3 -> 8, all 9 -> never). Test 10 therefore asserts a false expected value AND names its killing mutation backwards: it says "dropping the IsLegacyRound check ... makes v0.35.0's recorded history report all as never-converged", but KEEPING the check produces that result, because none of those rounds is legacy. Test 6 pins the contradiction inside the same release: it asserts all converges at round 9 on the same nine rounds. The two tests cannot both pass.
suggestion: IsLegacyRound answers "are this round's item ids comparable", not "was this round recorded before the reset shipped", and reusing it silently inherits a v0.30.0 boundary. Record a NEW marker at audit_record.go alongside IDScheme (a reset/round-schema stamp, or a tp version), define the boundary as "the first round carrying that stamp", and build test 10's fixture from rounds this release recorded plus older unstamped ones -- not from v0.35.0's history, which is stamped. Then test 6's replay is legal because the copied testdata carries no new stamp.

finding: §3 repairs round 4's missing-marker finding by naming a marker that already exists for a DIFFERENT release, so the prospectivity rule is a no-op and the reset is retroactive after all. `engine.IsLegacyRound` is `return r.IDScheme == ""` (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:503-505), and `IDScheme` is stamped `engine.IDSchemeSlug` by internal/cli/audit_record.go:213 on EVERY audit round recorded since v0.30.0 — its own struct comment (reviewstate.go:28-34) says so: 'Value "slug" for an audit round recorded under v0.30.0+ ... empty on a legacy round recorded before this release', where 'this release' is v0.30.0. Measured on the very corpus §3 argues from: all nine audit rounds in spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json carry "id_scheme": "slug", so `IsLegacyRound` is false for every one and §3's rule — 'applies the reset only from the first marked round onward' — starts at round 1. Their spec_hashes are r1=r2=a46f45c6, r3=c06544ea, r4=50be1428, r5=2dd780c6, r6=6f42a8eb, r7=r8=1259a4af, r9=54e031e6; the only two clean rounds are r8 and r9 and the hash moves between them, so `ConsecutiveCleanSince` returns 1 and at audit_clean_rounds 2 `ConvergedSince` is false. A converged, shipped cycle reports converged:false the moment this release installs — the exact retroactive outcome §3's 'Why the word alone will not do' paragraph says the marker prevents. The marker also cannot be repurposed: it is recorded on audit rounds only (reviewstate.go:33-34, asserted by cli/idscheme_marker_test.go:49), so a review-side reader of the same field would see every round as legacy.
suggestion: This release needs its own marker, not v0.30.0's. Add a per-round field stamped by --record from v0.37.0 forward (e.g. `hash_reset: true`, or a `recorded_by` version string) and state that the walk cuts at a boundary only when the NEWER of the two adjacent rounds carries it, so no history recorded before the upgrade can ever cut. Then state, as the worked example §3 already uses, what the reset returns on v0.35.0's nine rounds under the new marker (it must be the pre-reset 2, not 1). If reusing IsLegacyRound is genuinely intended, §3 must say that the reset applies to every audit round recorded since v0.30.0 and own the v0.35.0 regression as the release's stated behaviour.

finding: §3's repair picks a marker that marks the wrong release, and the corpus shows it changes nothing. §3 now says: 'tp already owns the pattern: `ReviewRound.IDScheme` plus `engine.IsLegacyRound` (`engine/reviewstate.go:503-505`) marks a round's vintage on the round itself. **`ConsecutiveCleanSince` treats a round `IsLegacyRound` reports as pre-marker the way `ConsecutiveClean` does -- no boundary -- and applies the reset only from the first marked round onward.**' Read at the cited lines, `IsLegacyRound(r) = r.IDScheme == ""`, and `engine.IDSchemeSlug` is documented in the same file (reviewstate.go:44-46) as 'the marker value recorded on a **v0.30.0+** audit round'; `audit_record.go:213` has stamped it on every audit round since. So the marker separates v0.30.0 from v0.29.0, not v0.37.0 from v0.36.0. Every audit round this release could plausibly be run against is already marked, so the reset is fully retroactive on every history that matters -- which is the exact outcome §3's next paragraph introduces the marker to prevent ('Deleting the word retroactive did not stop the mechanism being retroactive; the marker does'). Measured, not inferred: I walked all 15 recorded audit histories in spec/.tp-review/*/state.json computing ConsecutiveClean, ConsecutiveCleanSince-with-the-IsLegacyRound-check, and ConsecutiveCleanSince-without-it. **The check changes the answer in 0 of 15 histories.** v0.29.0 is the only marker-less history and its four rounds share one spec_hash, so even there the check is inert. And on v0.35.0 -- the history §3 and §2.1 both argue from -- the marked reset takes consecutive_clean from 2 to 1 (r8 hash 1259a4af, r9 hash 54e031e6, a boundary between the only two clean rounds), so §2.1's table row 'v0.35.0 | 9, converged | round 3 | round 9' is still falsified by §3 in the same file, exactly as it was before this round's repair. This is not round 4's finding restated: round 4 said prospectivity had no mechanism; this round supplied one, and the one supplied is measurably a no-op.
suggestion: `IsLegacyRound` cannot carry this. Either (a) record a NEW per-round marker written from v0.37.0 forward -- §3 may follow IDScheme's *pattern* but must not reuse its *value*, e.g. a `reset_scheme` field with `ConsecutiveCleanSince` treating an unmarked round as boundary-free -- and say plainly that this release adds a stored byte to `ReviewRound`; or (b) drop prospectivity, accept the retroactive reset, and rewrite §2.1's table under the composed rule (v0.35.0 becomes `blocking` 8 / `all` never, already simulated in §3's own paragraph) so the release's evidence and its mechanism agree. Whichever is chosen, add the assertion that discriminates: the same rounds with and without the marker must give different answers, on a fixture built for it rather than on v0.35.0's history, which cannot tell them apart.

finding: Test 10 names a killing mutation that does not kill, on the very input it names, and §5's own preamble is the standard it fails. Test 10: 'Prospectivity has a marker. A round that `engine.IsLegacyRound` reports as pre-marker contributes no boundary, so a history recorded before the upgrade keeps the `consecutive_clean` it had. The mutation that kills it: dropping the `IsLegacyRound` check, which makes v0.35.0's recorded history report `all` as never-converged.' Both halves are false against the corpus. (1) v0.35.0's nine audit rounds all carry `id_scheme: "slug"` (read from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json), so `IsLegacyRound` is false for every one of them: with the check present, v0.35.0's history ALREADY reports `all` as never-converged -- consecutive_clean falls 2 to 1 at the r8/r9 hash boundary. Dropping the check leaves that answer byte-identical, so the named mutation is not detectable on the named input. (2) 'a history recorded before the upgrade keeps the `consecutive_clean` it had' is false of the same history for the same reason: it does not keep it, it loses one. Computed across all 15 recorded audit histories, no input in this repository discriminates the two variants -- the only marker-less history, v0.29.0, has a single spec_hash across its four rounds, so the boundary rule is inert there whichever way the check goes. §5 opens 'Every test names the input that makes it fail, because four earlier drafts of this list contained a test that passed against unmodified tp'; test 10 is the fifth, and it is the test for the mechanism §3 added this round.
suggestion: Test 10 needs a fixture that is *constructed* to discriminate: two clean rounds at different `spec_hash` values with the marker absent on both (consecutive_clean stays 2) and the identical rounds with the marker present (falls to 1). State both arms in the test, since a one-arm assertion passes whatever the check does. Delete the v0.35.0 sentence, or replace it with the true statement: under §3 as written, v0.35.0's recorded history reports `all` as never-converged with the check in place, which is the finding §2.1 has to answer.

finding: Test 10's named killing mutation cannot fail, so the test passes against an implementation that omits the mechanism §3 exists to add. Test 10: 'The mutation that kills it: dropping the `IsLegacyRound` check, which makes v0.35.0's recorded history report `all` as never-converged.' Measured: all nine audit rounds in spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json carry "id_scheme": "slug", so `IsLegacyRound` (reviewstate.go:503-505, `r.IDScheme == ""`) returns FALSE for every one of them with the check in place. Keeping the check and dropping it therefore produce identical answers on the named input, and that answer is the mutant's answer — never-converged — in both. §5's own opening promise ('Every test names the input that makes it fail, because four earlier drafts of this list contained a test that passed against unmodified tp') is the rule this test breaks, and CLAUDE.md states it generally: the informative experiment is the one that could have failed. Test 10's other half is unwritable for the same reason: 'a history recorded before the upgrade keeps the `consecutive_clean` it had' has no instance in this repository, because no audit round tp has ever recorded lacks the marker — only a synthesised `ReviewRound{IDScheme: ""}` sequence exhibits the case, and a synthesised marker-less round is by construction a round no --record of any tp version produces on the audit path.

(a) A unit-level assertion over synthesised rounds — `ConsecutiveCleanSince` on `[{IDScheme:"", SpecHash:A, Clean:true}, {IDScheme:"", SpecHash:B, Clean:true}]` returns 2 while the same pair with the v0.37.0 marker returns 1 — which is a mutation the IsLegacyRound check actually survives. finding: Test 11 pins one command form and there are two write paths, so the test passes over an unfenced one -- and the unfenced one is the form tp's own shipped test already uses. finding: The fence added this round says `tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` exits 2 under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` "with the escalation hint the other fenced decisions use", and §5 test 11 pins "the escalation hint". Neither says which decision name. That name is not free-form: `tp escalate --decision` is a closed, validated set -- `skip-gate, raise-review-cap, raise-audit-cap, import-force, other` (`internal/cli/escalate.go:41`, refused by `IsEscalationDecision` at `:82`) -- and `escalationDecision(field)` in `internal/cli/unattended.go:19-27` maps only `review_max_rounds` and `audit_max_rounds`, returning `other` for everything else. So as specified, a unit refused on this field escalates as `decision: other`, the run stops with `stop_reason: escalation`, and the record the driver hands the operator is byte-indistinguishable from every other unnamed escalation: the operator must read the free-text `evidence` on every stop to learn what the run stopped for, which is exactly the per-stop round-trip the named decisions exist to remove. The alternative -- a sixth decision name -- is new surface on a validated enum plus its hint string, and the release budgets neither. §5 test 11 passes under both readings, so the choice is not forced by any test.
suggestion: Decide it in §2: either state that `audit_converge_on` escalates under the existing `other` and say why an unnamed stop is acceptable for it, or name the sixth decision (e.g. `relax-audit-convergence`), add it to `engine.EscalationDecisions()` in this release's scope alongside the fence, and make §5 test 11 assert the decision name rather than "the escalation hint".

finding: §2 and §5 test 11 fence one of the two commands that can write the field, and the unfenced one is the command §4's own guard test drives. `fenceWorkflowWrite` has exactly four call sites: internal/cli/set.go:414 and :428, and internal/cli/set_project.go:98 and :108. finding: §2 states the predicate over round cleanliness alone and never says whether `audit_converge_on` reaches the three other derived values `tp audit --record` emits from the same rows, all of which are severity-blind today. internal/engine/rolestreaks.go:128-142 `auditRoundOpenByRole` tallies a role's open rows through `AuditRowIsPass` and reads no severity at all; `RoleStreak.Open` and `RoleStreak.ConsecutiveClean` come from that tally (rolestreaks.go:107-108), and engine/speccoverage.go's `SpecCoverageCleanRounds` is derived from those streaks. So under `blocking`, an unchanged implementation records a round `clean: true` while the SAME payload reports `role_streaks: [{role: maintainability-conventions, consecutive_clean: 0, open: 3}]` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` unchanged. I cannot write acceptance for §2's task without that decision, and it is not cosmetic in either direction: Non-Goal 1's argument ('a severity-parity `--check` still exits 1 for exactly the rounds the gap is about') presupposes severity parity reaching the streak surface, while §2's text confines the field to `clean`. §2's own touch list ('16 production `.go` files') is the review-side count and contains neither rolestreaks.go nor speccoverage.go, because `review_converge_on` has no per-role streak surface to reach — so the audit twin's surface is strictly larger than the number §2 sizes it by.
suggestion: State it in §2 in one sentence, and give it a test. Either: '`audit_converge_on` scopes the round-level `clean` predicate only — `role_streaks`, `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` and `divergence` keep counting every non-`PASS` row, so a clean round under `blocking` can carry a non-zero `open`', with a §5 test asserting exactly that pairing so the apparent contradiction is pinned as intended; or 'the same predicate governs `auditRoundOpenByRole`', in which case add engine/rolestreaks.go and engine/speccoverage.go to the touch list and say what `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` means once it counts only blocking rows.

finding: §2's justification for the fence rests on a superlative its own next paragraph refutes. §2: 'This is the **first workflow field whose non-default value relaxes a gate**; `review_converge_on`'s weak value is its own default, so nothing has needed this before.' Two sentences later: 'the only workflow-write fence is `fenceWorkflowWrite(field string, requested float64)` in `internal/cli/unattended.go:56` -- **numeric by signature**, covering caps and command fields.' A cap fence exists precisely because raising a cap relaxes a gate. Verified in the shipped surface: `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`'s fence table carries '`tp set --workflow review_max_rounds=` / `audit_max_rounds=` **above** the resolved value | exit 2' and the same row for `run_max_*`, and REFERENCE.md's own explanation is 'an equal or lower value is accepted and exits 0, since lowering a budget cannot manufacture convergence' -- i.e. the raise is the relaxation. `review_max_rounds`, `audit_max_rounds` and the five `run_max_*` fields are all workflow fields whose non-default value relaxes a gate, and all seven are already fenced. The clause that IS true and that carries the whole mechanical argument is the narrower one: this is the first **string-valued** such field, which is exactly why a `float64` signature does not fit it. As written the sentence overstates the release's novelty, and it does so in the paragraph that answers 'why is the fence the content of this release' -- so a reader who checks the superlative finds it false and has no reason left for the paragraph. It also invites the wrong repair: 'widen the fence to string fields' reads as inventing a category when the category already exists and only its parameter type is wrong.
suggestion: Write 'the first **string-valued** workflow field whose non-default value relaxes a gate -- the seven cap fields already do, which is why `fenceWorkflowWrite` exists, and why its `float64` parameter is the whole problem'. That keeps the argument, makes it true, and names the fix as a signature change rather than a new concept.

finding: §2's new cost measurement puts "both `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md` and `skills/tp/SKILL.md`" in scope by filename and names no claim in either. Those two files are the bytes every agent loads every session, so a stale sentence there is not a documentation debt -- it is a wrong decision per agent per session, which is the most expensive unit of waste tp has.
